title: 7.2 Win Rate Versus Payoff
bodyHtml:
7.2 Win Rate Versus Payoff

Why This Matters

Beginners often chase one number:

win rate

They want to be right as often as possible.

But trading performance is not only about how often you win. It is also about:

  • how big your winners are;
  • how big your losers are.

A trader can win often and still lose money overall. A trader can win less often and still be profitable.

That is why win rate has to be reviewed together with payoff.

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • explain win rate and payoff in plain language;
  • understand why a high win rate can still hide a weak process;
  • review average wins and average losses together instead of chasing accuracy alone.

Two Numbers That Must Work Together

Term Plain-English meaning Why it matters
Win rate The percentage of trades that end as winners Shows how often your trade ideas work
Average win The typical size of your winners Shows what you make when you are right
Average loss The typical size of your losers Shows what you lose when you are wrong
Payoff ratio Average win compared with average loss Shows whether winners are large enough to cover losers

(Table alt-text: A four-row table explaining win rate, average win, average loss, and payoff ratio in simple language.)

Win rate answers:

how often did I win?

Payoff answers:

when I win, is it big enough compared with what I lose?

You need both answers.

A Simple Example

Look at these two traders:

Trader Win rate Average win Average loss Result over 10 trades
Trader A 80% USD 10 USD 100 8 small wins from quick FX or index trades = USD 80; 2 large losses from weak oil or gold management = USD 200; net = -USD 120
Trader B 40% USD 300 USD 100 4 larger wins from patient index, gold, or FX trades = USD 1,200; 6 capped losses = USD 600; net = USD 600

(Table alt-text: A two-row table showing that a trader with an 80 percent win rate can still lose money, while a trader with a 40 percent win rate can still make money if winners are larger than losers.)

Trader A feels more accurate. Trader B has the healthier performance math.

That is the central lesson.

Why This Goes Wrong for Beginners

The SEC has highlighted the disposition effect as a behavior that can hurt investment performance.

In plain language, that means:

  • holding losers too long;
  • selling winners too soon.

That behavior creates a dangerous pattern:

  • average losses grow;
  • average wins shrink;
  • the payoff ratio weakens.

A trader may still say:

but I win a lot

That does not fix the math.

One Simple Review Formula

You do not need advanced statistics to start reviewing properly.

One simple expectancy formula is:

expectancy per trade = (win rate x average win) - (loss rate x average loss)

You can use it after a sample of trades to ask:

  • Is my system making more when right than it loses when wrong?
  • Are my losses too large?
  • Are my wins too small because I exit too early?

The formula does not remove uncertainty. It helps you measure whether the process is viable.

What to Review Each Week or Month

  1. Count total trades.
  2. Count winners and losers.
  3. Calculate win rate.
  4. Calculate average win and average loss.
  5. Compare them honestly.
  6. Ask what behavior is damaging the numbers.

This is where journaling matters. If the numbers are weak, the journal should tell you why.

It should also tell you where.

Maybe the weak payoff came from:

  • cutting gold winners too early;
  • letting Brent losses run too long;
  • taking low-quality FX trades late in the session;
  • forcing stock-index entries during event risk.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Treating Win Rate as the Whole Story

Accuracy alone does not tell you whether the process makes money.

Mistake 2: Selling Winners Too Quickly

This can make the average win too small.

Mistake 3: Letting Losses Grow

This can make the average loss too large.

Mistake 4: Reviewing to Protect the Ego

The goal is diagnosis, not feeling smart.
learningOutcomes: explain win rate, average win, average loss, and payoff in plain language;
identify when a high win rate still hides poor performance math;
use simple expectancy review to diagnose behavior problems.
